THE QUIET SHORE

by Tomas Weir

CHAPTER I.

Some mornings the fog came in so thickly that the island seemed to float alone in a white room. Mara climbed the iron stairs of the lighthouse before the sun had cleared the water. There were nights when nothing passed at all, and the light kept faith with an empty sea. The radio crackled with forecasts read by a calm voice that had never seen the rock. In winter the waves threw stones as large as loaves against the door of the oil store. She learned the voices of the weather the way other people learn the voices of their neighbours.

The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted. The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted. Every ship that passed the rock was a story she would never hear the end of.

When the wind turned to the north the windows sang a single high note that lasted all night. In the evenings she read by the stove, a blanket over her knees and the cat asleep against her ankle. Her boots stood by the stove each night, toes towards the heat, like two tired dogs.

Below the gallery the sea moved in long grey ridges, patient as a herd of sleeping animals. Twice a year an inspector arrived with a clipboard and left with wet boots and nothing to complain about. She had stopped counting the days long ago and counted the seasons instead. She kept a jar of sea glass on the windowsill, green and white and one rare piece of blue. Their youngest child drew the lighthouse on the back of an envelope and left it pinned above the stove.

A gull settled on the rail, considered her with one yellow eye, and left without a sound. The lamp room smelled of brass polish, paraffin and the salt that crept in through every seam. In winter the waves threw stones as large as loaves against the door of the oil store. The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted. The almanac on the kitchen table listed the tides for a year she had not yet lived.

The almanac on the kitchen table listed the tides for a year she had not yet lived. The radio crackled with forecasts read by a calm voice that had never seen the rock. She painted the railings white every summer, and every winter the sea took the paint back. She kept a jar of sea glass on the windowsill, green and white and one rare piece of blue. Twice a year an inspector arrived with a clipboard and left with wet boots and nothing to complain about. A fishing family once sheltered with her for three days while a storm tore at the slates.

When the wind turned to the north the windows sang a single high note that lasted all night. Her hands knew the lamp better than her eyes did, and in the dark they never made a mistake. Spring came late to the island, first as a softening of the wind and then as birds. Spring came late to the island, first as a softening of the wind and then as birds.

Spring came late to the island, first as a softening of the wind and then as birds. The lamp room smelled of brass polish, paraffin and the salt that crept in through every seam. Twice a year an inspector arrived with a clipboard and left with wet boots and nothing to complain about. Spring came late to the island, first as a softening of the wind and then as birds.

In winter the waves threw stones as large as loaves against the door of the oil store. Far out on the horizon the lights of the trawlers moved like slow stars along the edge of the world. Her hands knew the lamp better than her eyes did, and in the dark they never made a mistake. Every ship that passed the rock was a story she would never hear the end of. The garden behind the cottage gave her potatoes, a few stubborn onions and, once, a single rose. The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted.

A fishing family once sheltered with her for three days while a storm tore at the slates. Her hands knew the lamp better than her eyes did, and in the dark they never made a mistake. Letters from the mainland arrived in bundles, and she read them in the order they were written. In winter the waves threw stones as large as loaves against the door of the oil store. When the lamp turned, its beam swept across the water like a slow hand smoothing a tablecloth.

CHAPTER II.

On clear days she could see the church tower on the mainland, small and certain as a pencil mark. The lamp room smelled of brass polish, paraffin and the salt that crept in through every seam. She liked the hour before dawn best, when the light was still working and the world was not. The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted. Below the gallery the sea moved in long grey ridges, patient as a herd of sleeping animals.

The almanac on the kitchen table listed the tides for a year she had not yet lived. The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted. Every ship that passed the rock was a story she would never hear the end of.

In the evenings she read by the stove, a blanket over her knees and the cat asleep against her ankle. The almanac on the kitchen table listed the tides for a year she had not yet lived. The supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, and the weather seldom permitted. The keeper before her father had carved his initials into the lintel above the lamp room door. The almanac on the kitchen table listed the tides for a year she had not yet lived. The radio crackled with forecasts read by a calm voice that had never seen the rock.

Every ship that passed the rock was a story she would never hear the end of. Some mornings the fog came in so thickly that the island seemed to float alone in a white room. Her coat hung on a nail by the door, stiff with the memory of a hundred crossings to the landing stage. At the turn of the tide the rocks below the lighthouse rang with a hollow, drumming sound. She had stopped counting the days long ago and counted the seasons instead.

Her hands knew the lamp better than her eyes did, and in the dark they never made a mistake. When the wind turned to the north the windows sang a single high note that lasted all night. The books on her shelf had swollen in the damp until their covers curled like dry leaves. She wrote the wind, the swell and the colour of the sky in the ledger her father had kept before her. Her boots stood by the stove each night, toes towards the heat, like two tired dogs.

On those mornings she wound the clockwork of the fog bell and counted the strokes under her breath. The lamp room smelled of brass polish, paraffin and the salt that crept in through every seam. On those mornings she wound the clockwork of the fog bell and counted the strokes under her breath. She liked the hour before dawn best, when the light was still working and the world was not. The books on her shelf had swollen in the damp until their covers curled like dry leaves.

Her hands knew the lamp better than her eyes did, and in the dark they never made a mistake. Sometimes she spoke aloud to the lamp, and it seemed only polite that it never interrupted.
